title: From Slippery Phone to the U.S. Navy: Missy Kelly's Product Playbook
guestBio: Missy Kelly is the Co-Founder and CEO of CatTongue Grips, a 7-figure global brand of patented non-abrasive, non-slip solutions now used by Walmart, SpaceX, Blue Origin, and the U.S. Navy. She is also the founder of Born for Impact, a speaking and coaching platform for entrepreneurs, and a WBENC national forum member and former Chair of the WBEC-West Utah Forum. Missy is featured in the upcoming Women Gone Wild: Leadership Edition and is passionate about helping everyday people recognize ordinary problems as world-changing opportunities.
excerpt: Missy Kelly had zero manufacturing experience when her husband's slippery phone sparked a patented non-slip material now trusted by Walmart, SpaceX, and the U.S. Navy. In this episode, she breaks down the real playbook — prototypes, 150 emails to Walmart, and the inner work that makes it all sustainable. If you've ever thought "someone should fix this," this episode is your sign that the someone is you.
metaDescription: Missy Kelly turned a slippery phone into a 7-figure product empire. Learn her playbook for patents, corporate sales, and entrepreneur identity on The Manage Her®.
keyTakeaways: If you need something that doesn't exist yet, thousands of other people probably need it too — your personal frustration is a market signal worth following.
You don't need an MBA, a manufacturing background, or a perfect plan; you need to take the first step before you feel certain, and let each step reveal the next.
Your customer is your most powerful sales engine — listening closely to how they're using your product will show you markets you never would have discovered on your own.
Asking every corporate buyer 'what made you take this meeting with me?' is a simple question that unlocks the exact language and logic you need to close the deal.
Corporate and government contracts are a marathon, not a sprint — always ask each contact how they want to be followed up with so your persistence reads as professionalism.
Separating your identity from your company's daily performance is not a luxury; it's the prerequisite for sustainable growth and the only way both you and your business can fully expand.
Perfectionism is not a productivity trait — it is an outer symptom of feeling unworthy, and naming it honestly is the first step to moving through it.

pullQuotes.text: Zero. That's what I knew about manufacturing, patents, and distribution when I started. Zero. And I did it anyway.
Your customer is your sales engine. They will lead you into rooms you never even knew to knock on.
Ask every buyer: 'What made you take the meeting with me?' That one question will tell you everything you need to steer the conversation.

Be whole inside regardless of what the company is doing. That's when both of you expand.

quiz.title: What Kind of Entrepreneur Are You — Really?
quiz.description: You have ideas. You have drive. But the way you build, sell, and sustain yourself is deeply personal. This quiz helps you understand your entrepreneurial wiring — and shows you exactly what Missy's story has to offer someone like you.

A.name: The Visionary Builder
A.description: You see the gap in the market before anyone else does, and your energy in the early stages is almost electric. The challenge is that you can get ahead of yourself — ten ideas deep before prototype one is finished. Missy's nine-iteration journey is a love letter to your wiring: your instinct is right, and the execution just needs a little more patience than inspiration. This episode will show you how to channel that vision into a product the world can actually hold.

B.name: The Strategic Closer
B.description: You are most alive when there's a deal on the table and a decision-maker in the room. You think in systems, you track follow-up cadences, and you genuinely enjoy the long game of corporate sales — even when it takes 150 emails. Missy's playbook for landing Walmart and the U.S. Navy was made for your brain. This episode gives you the exact language and posture that turns a warm lead into a signed contract.

C.name: The Heart-Led Founder
C.description: You started your business because you genuinely wanted to change something — for a person, a community, a problem that mattered. Revenue matters, but it has never been the whole point. The risk for you is over-giving and under-charging, and tying your self-worth to whether your customers are happy. Missy's Impact Matrix and her hard-won wisdom about separating identity from company were written for you. This episode will help you protect the very thing that makes you brilliant.

D.name: The Reluctant Innovator
D.description: You have been circling an idea — maybe for months, maybe for years — telling yourself you'll move when you know more, when the timing is better, when you feel ready. The truth is, you are more prepared than you think, and the certainty you are waiting for only comes after the first step, not before. Missy knew zero about manufacturing when she started, and she built a global brand anyway. This episode will be the nudge you didn't know you needed.

questions.question: When a problem frustrates you enough to say 'someone should really fix this,' what usually happens next?

options.text: I start sketching out how I would fix it — often before I finish the sentence.
I research whether a market exists for the solution before I get too excited.
I think about all the people this problem is affecting and feel a pull to help.
I file it away in the back of my mind and revisit it when I feel more ready.

questions.question: You just got a meeting with a major corporate buyer. The night before, you are most likely to:

options.text: Stay up late building a deck with bold visuals and a compelling origin story.
Review their procurement history and prepare a tight, data-backed value proposition.
Think about the problem their employees or customers are facing and how your solution genuinely helps.
Second-guess whether you are ready and rehearse every possible objection they might raise.

questions.question: When your business has a hard month, how does it tend to affect you personally?

options.text: I pivot fast — I don't like sitting in it, so I'm already chasing the next idea.
I analyze what happened and build a plan before I let myself feel too much.
It hits harder than it probably should — the business and I are pretty intertwined.
I quietly wonder if this is a sign I should have waited until I was more prepared.

questions.question: A customer uses your product in a completely unexpected way and tells you about it. Your first instinct is:

options.text: Excitement — this could be an entirely new product line or market.
Curiosity about the size of that adjacent market and what it would take to enter it.
Gratitude — I love when a customer trusts me enough to share something like that.
Hesitation — I wouldn't want to expand before I've truly mastered what I already have.

questions.question: When you think about the legacy you want your work to leave, what feels most true?

options.text: I want to be known for building something no one had imagined before.
I want to be known for executing with precision and growing something that lasts.
I want to be known for the lives I changed, more than the revenue I generated.
I want to be known for finally betting on myself — and proving it was worth it.

questions.question: Be honest: where does perfectionism show up most in your work?

options.text: I launch fast and fix later — perfectionism isn't really my problem, but follow-through sometimes is.
I can get stuck refining a pitch or a process past the point of diminishing returns.
I delay sharing my work because I worry it won't land the way I need it to for the people I care about.
I use 'it's not ready yet' as a reason not to start — and I know it, even as I'm doing it.

content:
There is a moment most entrepreneurs can name exactly — the moment a small, ordinary frustration flickers into something bigger. For Missy Kelly, that moment was her husband fumbling with a slippery phone. For you, it might be something you've tripped over a hundred times and quietly thought, "why hasn't someone fixed this?" This episode is your answer: because that someone is you.

Missy Kelly is the Co-Founder and CEO of CatTongue Grips, a 7-figure global brand built on a patented non-abrasive, non-slip material now trusted by Walmart, SpaceX, Blue Origin, and the U.S. Navy. She started with zero manufacturing experience, zero distribution knowledge, and zero connections in the corporate procurement world. What she had was a clear problem, a relentless willingness to take the next step, and the emotional intelligence to build a business without losing herself in it.

The Nine Prototypes Nobody Talks About

Here's what the highlight reel leaves out: Missy's first product was not the product. It took nine iterations — nine rounds of testing, failing, and refining — before CatTongue Grips became the material it is today. The original inspiration was skateboard grip tape, which gripped but also shredded skin. The mission became finding something that held on without tearing up. That nuance — non-abrasive and non-slip — is what eventually made it irreplaceable on wheelchair footplates, shower grab rails, and F-35 fighter jet maintenance walkways.

If you are sitting on an idea and waiting until you know enough to start, Missy's nine prototypes are your permission slip. You are not supposed to know how yet. The how reveals itself in motion, not in planning.

The Customer Who Changed Everything

One of the most powerful moments in this conversation comes courtesy of Earl — a trucker Missy had never met — whose offhand suggestion about grip placement on industrial equipment opened a door into aerospace and military contracts she hadn't even considered. Earl didn't have a title. He didn't have procurement authority. He just had a problem, and he told Missy about it honestly.

This is the lesson beneath the lesson: your customer is your sales engine. The buyers in your pipeline will tell you, if you listen closely enough, exactly where your product needs to go next. Missy didn't push her way into the defense sector. She followed her customer there. That posture — curious, listening, genuinely service-oriented — is what turns a consumer product into a government contract.

The Question That Opens Every Corporate Door

Missy shares one of the most disarmingly simple sales strategies you will ever hear: when you get a meeting with a corporate buyer, ask them, "What made you take the meeting with me?" That's it. That single question tells you how they found you, what problem they're hoping you solve, and exactly how to frame the rest of the conversation. It turns a pitch into a dialogue. It signals confidence without arrogance. And it gives you intelligence no amount of pre-meeting research could match.

The 150-email campaign that eventually landed a Walmart partnership didn't start with volume — it started with understanding. Missy didn't spam a contact; she built a relationship at the pace that contact set, always asking how they wanted to hear from her next. Persistence without permission is noise. Persistence with it is partnership.

The Inner Work Is the Work

What makes this episode stand apart isn't just the business mechanics — it's Missy's unflinching honesty about the identity work that has to happen underneath the strategy. She introduces the Impact Matrix: a framework built on intention, mindset, purpose, action, conviction, and trust. And she's clear that none of the external elements function properly if the internal ones are fractured.

A founder whose ego is fused to her company's revenue number, her latest press mention, or whether the product sold well at the trade show is a founder on the fastest road to burnout. When the company has a bad quarter, she has a bad quarter. When the deal falls through, so does she. Missy has lived this, and she talks about it with the earned authority of someone who has done the uncomfortable work of separating who she is from what she built.

She also names perfectionism with surgical precision: it is not a work-ethic trait. It is not ambition in disguise. It is, at its root, an outer symptom of feeling unworthy — and dressing it up as a high standard doesn't make it less costly. If you've ever stalled on launching, pitching, or publishing because it wasn't quite ready, this part of the conversation is for you.

You Don't Need a Bigger Company to Play This Game

One of the most permission-giving things about Missy's story is its scale at the start. She was not backed by venture capital. She did not come from a manufacturing family. She learned what a patent was after she needed one. And she still landed contracts with some of the most demanding procurement organizations in the world — because she showed up prepared, followed up with integrity, and built a product that solved a real problem beautifully.

The WBENC certification she holds — Women's Business Enterprise National Council — opened corporate doors that cold outreach alone couldn't. But she is also honest about what it doesn't do: it doesn't close the deal for you. That still takes the relationship, the product, and the follow-through. Certification is a key that gets you to the door. You still have to knock.

Missy Kelly's story is proof that the gap between "someone should fix this" and "I built a seven-figure company fixing this" is filled not with special credentials, but with a willingness to take the next imperfect step. If you've been sitting on an idea, this episode is 91 minutes of the most practical, emotionally honest, and genuinely energizing permission you will find anywhere.

Hit play. Then go take that first step.
